Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty Images Politics Nigel Farage set for decisive but arguably empty victory in Clacton Leader of Reform UK on course to defeat Count Binface and an assortment of fringe candidates as polls close in Essex Peter Walker Senior political correspondent Thu 13 Aug 2026 17.56 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 18.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Voting has closed in one of the UK’s more unusual and least tense byelections, with Nigel Farage set for a decisive if arguably empty victory against dozens of independent, fringe, extreme or otherwise oddball opponents. The Reform UK leader sought re-election to his Clacton seat in early July in an attempt to regain the political initiative following weeks of scrutiny over gifts he received and other aspects of his financial affairs. He framed the byelection as a chance for local voters to show their disdain for mainstream politics in a “people versus the establishment” contest, but was caught out after all the other main parties declined to stand candidates. Farage, 62, was instead left competing against a vast if decidedly niche field of 33 other hopefuls, including 20 independents, several representatives from tiny parties and no fewer than three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony party. The result, due to be announced from around 6am on Friday, will inevitably be a clear Farage win, with the only question being his margin of victory over Count Binface , the self-styled campaigning alien who is the most prominent of his opponents. View image in fullscreen Nigel Farage poses with a pint in a Clacton pub beer garden. Photograph: Victoria Jones/Shutterstock While Reform will necessarily style the result as a clear endorsement of Farage’s record in the Essex seat, and of his tactic in calling the byelection, opponents will seize on any signs of a lower-than-expected majority or a slim turnout. Farage is being investigated by the parliamentary standards watchdog over allegations he failed to declare gifts and donations, including a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian. The process was paused when he resigned as an MP, but will resume once he is re-elected. If he is found to have breached declaration rules and suspended from the House of Commons, this could trigger a second byelection, which the other main parties would contest. While Farage insists he has relished a summer of knocking on doors in his constituency, he has been less visible on the national political stage – in part because of rules connected to how broadcasters must ensure balance during elections. Farage has insisted he did not need to declare the £5m from Harborne as it was given in advance of his return as Reform leader before the 2024 election. He has, however, given a series of explanations for the gift, including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit. The parliamentary inquiry is also looking into allegations that Farage was financially supported by the crypto gambler and convicted fraudster George Cottrell , a close friend, after the Sunday Times reported that Cottrell’s support included security and social media staff who worked on Farage’s online content in the year before he was elected. The 34-candidate field in the Clacton byelection is a UK record, beating the July 2008 contest in Haltemprice and Howden, East Yorkshire, regained by the Conservative MP David Davis after he resigned his seat and stood again as a protest over civil liberties. https://www.publishersweekly.com:443/pw/.text: Connecting Jews Around the Globe: PW Talks with Dóra Korányi and Sebastián Mizrahi By Leonard Picker | Sep 01, 2026 Loading the Elevenlabs Text to Speech AudioNative Player... Dóra Korányi, a Hungarian Jew, and her husband, Sebastián Mizrahi, who was raised in Venezuela by Argentinian parents of Syrian-Jewish and Russian-Jewish descent, wanted to make the history and traditions of all kinds of Jewish communities available online. So, they founded the online platform Qesher (which means "connection" in Hebrew) in 2020 with an international virtual lecture series. The platform has now grown now into book of 18 essays, Jewish Voices from Around the World: Tiles of a Mosaic (Vallentine Mitchell, Nov.), detailing some of the diverse perspectives featured on Qesher, including contributions by Jews from Uganda, Cuba, India, Libya and Curaçao. Why did you start Qesher? Dóra Korányi: I'm a psychologist by training, but I used to guide tours in the Jewish quarter of Budapest as a hobby. When the pandemic hit, I stopped doing that, and Sebastián had to stop organizing a Sephardic heritage tour in Spain. We thought, we have all this knowledge; let's do something online. First, we created just a series of five online lectures about the unique history, culture, and people of Jewish communities from people that we knew. I did my talk about Budapest, and then we knew someone from Spain, and from Turkey, from Bulgaria, and from Finland. How did this project grow into a book that includes Latin American, European, North African, Middle Eastern, Indian, and South African writers? DK: Most of our audience ended up being from North America, people who knew their Jewish roots were from different countries, but who knew very little of what's going on in that country now, or the history. Because there was so much interest, we looked for more people who can speak about other Jewish communities. It snowballed from there, and, within months, those lectures led to the creation of Qesher and the book. How did you choose contributors? Sebastián Mizrahi: We wanted this book to emphasize Jewish communities whose stories are less often told, so that readers from such communities could find, through this book, both something they can personally connect to, and things that were totally new to them. DK: We looked for contributors who really have deep roots in a place, who could include their family stories. But our aim is that someone who reads it will have the sensation of the variety of the Jewish communities, of Jewish languages and of Jewish histories. What do you find in common among the experiences of these far-flung communities, as varied as Sephardic Jews of Spanish and Portuguese descent and Jews with ancestry in Europe or Russia? SM: There are patterns that kept repeating, of exile and forced migrations, of how specific places received migrants from different communities that end up connecting, for example, leading to marriages between Sephardic and Ashkenazi Jews. What are some unexpected things you learned in doing this book? SM: Two communities placed such an emphasis on pronunciation that it caused serious internal rifts in them. Both the Jewish communities of Curacao, a Dutch colony, and Amsterdam experienced splits over a mispronounced syllable—whether the last word of the blessing over the wine, the Kiddush, should be pronounced "hageffen," or "haggafen." In Curacao, one faction even appealed to the king of Holland, seeking approval to found their own separate Jewish community. After their request was denied, that faction founded a second, unofficial and unauthorized Jewish community. They just prayed in their homes. This group eventually disappeared. DK: That essay illustrated how a kind of religious exactness had such a big role in their lives, which certainly wasn't the case everywhere. In Hungary, where I was born, for example, it's completely accepted in most communities that if your father's Jewish and you want to be Jewish, you can be Jewish, whereas traditionally, to be Jewish, someone must have a Jewish mother. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/02/uzbe.text: The biggest Chess Olympiad in history brought almost 400 teams from around the world to Samarkand, where host nation Uzbekistan won gold in the Open competition after defeating Ukraine in the final round.Uzbekistan won its first Chess Olympiad title in India's Chennai in 2022 and followed it with bronze in Budapest two years later.“This is our second Olympiad victory. Winning it at home feels different,” Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov said. “I think we played the tournament at the highest level.”Sindarov’s next major test will come later this year. After winning the Candidates Tournament, he will challenge India’s Gukesh Dommaraju for the world title in Geneva from 22 November to 12 December.Both players will be 20 when the match begins, making it the youngest World Championship contest in chess history.How the Chess Olympiad worksOrganised by the International Chess Federation (FIDE), the Chess Olympiad is the leading international team competition in chess.Unlike most major chess tournaments, players compete for their countries rather than only for themselves.Four players from one national team face four from another at the same time, with their individual results combined to determine the result between the two countries.Teams compete over 11 rounds, facing different opponents as the tournament progresses.Uzbekistan finished the competition with 20 of 22 possible match points, winning 10 of its 11 matches. Among the teams it defeated were defending champions India, China and the top-seeded US. Its only loss came against eventual bronze medallists Germany.Uzbekistan claims second Open titleNodirbek Abdusattorov was another key member of the winning team. Playing on Uzbekistan’s first board, meaning he generally faced the strongest player from each opposing team, he completed the Chess Olympiad without losing a game and received an individual gold medal for his performance.“I think we can now confidently say that Uzbekistan is unrivalled in the world of chess,” Abdusattorov said after the victory.India finished with silver, while Germany took bronze.For Germany, the result marked its first Open team medal at a Chess Olympiad since 2000, when it won silver in Istanbul.“I think it’s by far the best Olympiad we’ve had in recent years, at least as long as I’ve been playing,” German grandmaster Vincent Keymer told Euronews.Several European countries also finished near the top, with Hungary, France and Spain all placing inside the top 10, alongside Azerbaijan and Armenia.In the women’s competition, China won gold, Kazakhstan finished second and defending champions India took bronze.Indian grandmaster Koneru Humpy was part of the bronze-medal-winning team.“There is a lot of attention from all the spectators and followers, and this is one of the widely followed tournaments from all over the world,” Humpy told Euronews.The biggest Olympiad yetThe final field included 205 teams in the Open and 189 in the Women’s competition.For almost two weeks, hundreds of games were played simultaneously in the same competition hall, bringing national teams from around the world together in Samarkand.The tournament also coincided with a change at the top of international chess. Timur Turlov, then president of the Kazakhstan Chess Federation, was elected president of FIDE during the federation’s General Assembly in Samarkand. At 38, he became the youngest person ever elected to the post.“The interest in the game is definitely rising year over year,” Turlov told Euronews. “It’s not just a professional sport. It’s a sport which is getting more and more popular almost everywhere.”At the end of the tournament, the Olympiad flag was handed to representatives of the United Arab Emirates.Abu Dhabi will host the 47th Chess Olympiad in 2028.
